projects.subject: economics
projects.title: The Metro Fare Dilemma
projects.mission: A city metro line tested five different fares. The operator wants the highest profit, the city wants enough passengers to justify the service, and then a fuel price shock raises costs. Investigate how passengers respond to fares, separate revenue from profit, and recommend a fare and subsidy that satisfy every condition.

sections.title: Demand and elasticity
sections.content: When the fare rises, the number of passengers usually falls. Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly: Ed = (% change in quantity demanded) ÷ (% change in price). If the size of Ed is greater than 1, demand is elastic. If it is less than 1, demand is inelastic.

sections.title: Revenue depends on elasticity
sections.content: Total revenue is fare × passengers. When demand is inelastic, a fare rise increases revenue because passengers fall by a smaller percentage than the fare rises. When demand is elastic, a fare rise reduces revenue.

sections.title: Revenue is not profit
sections.content: Profit = total revenue − total cost. A fare that maximises revenue may not maximise profit once the cost of carrying each passenger is included. A subsidy paid per passenger counts as extra income for the operator and as a cost for the city.

levels.title: Read the Fare Experiment

questions.prompt: The fare trial data records daily passengers at five fares. When the fare was raised from ₹10 to ₹15, what happened to passengers and to daily revenue?
options: Passengers fell from 1200 to 1000, but revenue rose from ₹12,000 to ₹15,000.
Passengers fell from 1200 to 1000, and revenue fell from ₹12,000 to ₹10,000.
Passengers rose from 1000 to 1200, and revenue rose from ₹12,000 to ₹15,000.
Passengers stayed at 1200, but revenue rose from ₹12,000 to ₹15,000.
questions.answer: Passengers fell from 1200 to 1000, but revenue rose from ₹12,000 to ₹15,000.
questions.explanation: At ₹10, revenue = 10 × 1200 = ₹12,000. At ₹15, revenue = 15 × 1000 = ₹15,000. Passengers fell, yet revenue rose.
hints: Revenue is fare multiplied by the number of passengers.
Calculate it for both rows in the trial data.

questions.prompt: Raising the fare from ₹25 to ₹30 reduced revenue from ₹15,000 to ₹12,000, yet raising it from ₹10 to ₹15 increased revenue. Which explanation fits the data?
options: At the higher fares, the percentage fall in passengers is larger than the percentage rise in the fare.
At higher fares, passengers stop responding to fare changes.
The operator's costs fall as the fare rises, which lowers revenue.
A ₹5 rise is always too small to affect revenue.
questions.answer: At the higher fares, the percentage fall in passengers is larger than the percentage rise in the fare.
questions.explanation: From ₹10 to ₹15 the fare rose 50% while passengers fell about 16.7%. From ₹25 to ₹30 the fare rose 20% while passengers fell about 33.3%. Revenue rose in the first case and fell in the second.
hints: Compare percentage changes, not rupee changes.
Which is larger in each case: the percentage change in fare or in passengers?

levels.evidenceUse: Use fare_trial_data.csv to compare passengers and revenue at the different fares.
levels.simulationUse: Move the fare slider and watch passengers and revenue change together.

levels.title: Measure the Response

questions.prompt: The fare was raised from ₹25 to ₹30. By what percentage did daily passengers fall?
questions.explanation: Passengers fell from 600 to 400. The change is (400 − 600) / 600 = −33.3%, so the fall is 33.3%.
hints: A percentage change is the change divided by the starting value.
Use the passenger numbers at ₹25 and ₹30.

questions.prompt: Between ₹25 and ₹30 the fare rose by 20% and passengers fell by 33.3%. Which description of demand in this range is correct?
options: Elastic (size of Ed about 1.67), so a fare rise reduces revenue.
Inelastic (size of Ed about 0.6), so a fare rise increases revenue.
Unitary elastic (size of Ed equal to 1), so revenue is unchanged.
Perfectly inelastic (Ed equal to 0), so passengers do not respond.
questions.answer: Elastic (size of Ed about 1.67), so a fare rise reduces revenue.
questions.explanation: Ed = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price = 33.3 ÷ 20 ≈ 1.67 in size. This is greater than 1, so demand is elastic and revenue falls when the fare rises, as the data shows.
hints: Divide the percentage change in passengers by the percentage change in fare.
Decide whether the size of the result is above or below 1.

questions.prompt: If the metro charges ₹20, what is the daily revenue?
questions.explanation: At ₹20 there are 800 passengers, so revenue = 20 × 800 = ₹16,000.
hints: Find the number of passengers at ₹20 in the trial data.
Multiply by the fare.

levels.evidenceUse: Use the passenger numbers in fare_trial_data.csv for each calculation.
levels.simulationUse: Compare your percentage changes and revenue with the simulation readouts.

levels.title: Revenue Is Not Profit

questions.prompt: Looking only at total revenue, which tested fare gives the operator the highest daily revenue?
hints: Calculate fare × passengers for each tested fare.

questions.prompt: Using the baseline cost per passenger from the operator memo, which tested fare gives the highest daily profit?
questions.explanation: With a cost of ₹8 per passenger, profit = (fare − 8) × passengers: ₹7,000 at ₹15, ₹9,600 at ₹20, ₹10,200 at ₹25 and ₹8,800 at ₹30. The highest is ₹10,200 at ₹25.
hints: Profit per passenger is the fare minus the cost of carrying that passenger.
Multiply the profit per passenger by the number of passengers.

questions.prompt: The authority requires at least 800 passengers per day, which rules out the profit-maximising fare. How much daily profit does the operator give up by charging the fare that keeps 800 passengers instead of the profit-maximising fare? Use the baseline cost.
questions.explanation: At ₹20 the profit is (20 − 8) × 800 = ₹9,600. At ₹25 the profit is (25 − 8) × 600 = ₹10,200. The operator gives up ₹10,200 − ₹9,600 = ₹600 per day.
hints: Find which fare still keeps 800 passengers.
Compare its profit with the profit you found in the previous question.

levels.evidenceUse: Use operator_cost_memo.txt for the cost per passenger and transport_authority_policy.txt for the passenger requirement.
levels.simulationUse: Use the simulation's profit readout to compare the revenue-maximising and profit-maximising fares.

levels.title: The Fuel Price Shock

questions.prompt: After the fuel price rise, the cost per passenger changes as stated in the operator memo. If the metro keeps the ₹20 fare with no subsidy, what is the daily profit?
questions.explanation: The new cost is ₹16 per passenger. Profit = (20 − 16) × 800 = ₹3,200.
hints: Use the updated cost per passenger, not the baseline cost.

questions.prompt: The authority requires the operator to earn at least the minimum daily profit stated in the policy. At the ₹20 fare, what is the smallest whole-rupee subsidy per passenger that achieves this?
questions.explanation: The operator needs at least ₹4,000. Without subsidy it earns ₹3,200. A subsidy of ₹s per passenger adds 800 × s, so 3,200 + 800s ≥ 4,000, which gives s ≥ 1.
hints: Find the shortfall between the required profit and the current profit.
The subsidy is paid for every passenger carried.

questions.prompt: The authority needs at least 800 passengers per day, the operator needs at least the minimum daily profit, and the city can pay at most the subsidy budget stated in the policy. Which option should be approved?
options: Fare ₹20 with a ₹1 subsidy per passenger
Fare ₹15 with a ₹5 subsidy per passenger
questions.answer: Fare ₹20 with a ₹1 subsidy per passenger
questions.explanation: Fare ₹30 earns (30 − 16) × 400 = ₹5,600 but carries only 400 passengers, below the minimum of 800. Fare ₹20 with no subsidy earns ₹3,200, below ₹4,000. Fare ₹20 with a ₹1 subsidy earns (20 + 1 − 16) × 800 = ₹4,000, carries 800 passengers and costs the city ₹800. Fare ₹15 with a ₹5 subsidy earns (15 + 5 − 16) × 1000 = ₹4,000 and carries 1000 passengers, but the subsidy would cost ₹5,000, above the ₹2,000 budget.
hints: Test each option against all three conditions: passengers, operator profit and city subsidy cost.
The subsidy cost is the subsidy per passenger multiplied by passengers.

levels.evidenceUse: Use the updated cost in operator_cost_memo.txt and the three conditions in transport_authority_policy.txt.
levels.simulationUse: Enter each option's fare and subsidy in the simulation and read the passengers, profit and subsidy cost before deciding.

requiredEvidence.instruction: Read every required file and use its information while solving the mission. The evidence is part of the investigation.

files.purpose: Compare daily passengers at five tested fares.
Read the cost of carrying a passenger, the definition of daily profit and the cost update after the fuel price rise.
files.content: Variable cost of carrying one passenger (baseline): ₹8. Daily profit = daily revenue − (cost per passenger × passengers carried). Any subsidy received is added to the operator's income. Cost update: after the fuel price rise and a new safety-attendant rule, the cost of carrying one passenger rises to ₹16.

files.purpose: Read the public-service requirement, the operator's minimum profit and the subsidy budget.
files.content: Public-service requirement: at least 800 passengers per day. Under the updated cost, the operator must earn at least ₹4,000 profit per day (including any subsidy) to keep the line running. Subsidy is paid per passenger carried. City subsidy budget for this route: at most ₹2,000 per day.

requiredSimulation.description: Interactive economics simulation of a metro line. Controls: fare, cost per passenger and subsidy per passenger. It displays daily passengers, revenue, profit, subsidy cost to the city, an elastic / inelastic indicator for the current fare range and a status for each policy condition.
requiredSimulation.integrationComment: Use the simulation to see how passengers, revenue, profit and subsidy cost respond together, to find where revenue and profit peak, and to test every option under the updated cost against all three policy conditions.
